q1: SELECT b.name AS bar, COUNT(DISTINCT f.drinker) AS num_drinker, AVG(s.price) AS avg_price, (SELECT f1.drinker FROM frequents AS f1 WHERE f1.bar = b.name ORDER BY f1.times_a_week DESC, f1.drinker ASC LIMIT 1) AS most_reg_drinker FROM bar AS b LEFT JOIN frequents AS f ON b.name = f.bar LEFT JOIN serves AS s ON b.name = s.bar GROUP BY b.name ORDER BY num_drinker DESC, b.name ASC
q2: WITH barList AS (SELECT bar.name AS bar, frequents.drinker, serves.beer, serves.price, frequents.times_a_week FROM bar FULL OUTER JOIN frequents ON bar.name = frequents.bar FULL OUTER JOIN serves ON bar.name = serves.bar) SELECT bar, COALESCE(COUNT(DISTINCT drinker), 0) AS distinct_drinkers, COALESCE(AVG(price), NULL) AS avg_price, COALESCE((SELECT drinker FROM frequents WHERE bar = barList.bar ORDER BY times_a_week DESC, drinker LIMIT 1), NULL) AS name FROM barList GROUP BY barList.bar ORDER BY distinct_drinkers DESC, name DESC

explanation: Q1 and Q2 are not semantically equivalent because they handle the JOINs differently. Q1 uses LEFT JOINs, which means it will include all bars from the Bar table, even if there are no corresponding entries in the Frequents or Serves tables. Q2, on the other hand, uses a FULL OUTER JOIN, which means it will include all bars from the Bar table, as well as all entries from the Frequents and Serves tables, even if there are no corresponding bars. This difference in JOIN behavior can lead to different results when calculating the number of drinkers and the average price.
counterexample_dsp: The test data should include a bar that has no corresponding entries in the Frequents or Serves tables. This will trigger the difference in results between Q1 and Q2.
